newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo can ill afford to ignore its new neighbours.
newsitem.headline: Congo can ill afford to ignore its new neighbours.

text.p: Diminutive Congo and Zaire's ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, its neighbour for over three decades, were good friends.
Now that he has moved out, whatever it might feel about its new neighbours, it can ill afford to ignore them.
Congo's President Pascal Lissouba, a personal friend of Mobutu, has yet to acknowledge Laurent Kabila, the new man in charge.
Like it or not, diplomats and government officials say, he has to be pragmatic and to come to terms with him -- and not leave it too long.
"For reasons of state I think they will establish relations. Congo cannot decline to recognise Zaire even if it wants to," said one senior government official who would not be named.
The Republic of Congo and the Democratic Republic of Congo -- Kabila's new name for Zaire -- were founded by competing colonialists France and Belgium's King Leopold in the 1880s.
Congo, with a population of three million has little more than half as many people as the Zaire capital. Zaire's total population tops 40 million.
Congo's government moved swiftly to ensure the departure of Mobutu family members who fled to Brazzaville as Kabila's fighters took power in Kinshasa on Saturday after a seven-month war.

The clan, including Mobutu's son army Captain Mobutu Kongolo, nicknamed Saddam Hussein, were bundled onto a flight as soon as a country could be found to take them, and joined the former president in Togo.

"In the end it is a matter of not giving Kabila's men a pretext for destabilising Congo by arguing that the former soldiers and barons of the MPR (Mobutu's party) are in Brazzaville," said Congo's daily Le Temps newspaper.
But Mobutu's family is not the only potential source of friction with Congo's new neighbours.
It has also become the destination of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees who trekked 1,600 km (1,000 miles) away from where the rebels launched their campaign, fearing for their lives.

The Hutus were the remnants of those who quit refugee camps on Zaire's eastern border with Rwanda when the Tutsi-dominated rebels attacked with barely concealed help of Rwanda's army, which is also dominated by Tutsis.
The Hutus arriving in Congo may well include soldiers of the Hutu former Rwandan army and extremist militias who carried out the 1994 genocide of at least 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda.
Another potential source of friction is Lissouba's good relations with former colonial power France, frequently accused by Kabila of trying to support Mobutu against the rebels.
In the short term, however, Kabila may be too busy at home to turn his attention to his much smaller neighbour.

"I see Kabila being in more of a hurry to set up cooperation agreements than to demonstrate unpleasant regional ambitions," said Roland Marchal of the Paris-based think-tank Centre d'Etudes et de Recherches Internationale.
But Lissouba's position is especially delicate in the run-up to multiparty presidential elections scheduled for July.

Political parties in Congo are based almost exclusively around ethnic groups. Past elections have led to bloodshed on the streets -- clashes between tribal-political militias after disputed 1993 elections killed an estimated 2,000 people.
Lissouba's officials are keen to head off anything that threatens to increase the political temperature.
"It's up to Lissouba to establish relations as quickly as he can because he may have little time to lose," one commented.
